edges.description: Aberrant transcripts reduce the pool of functional COX4I1.
Loss of a core structural subunit impairs complex IV biogenesis.
COX4I1 deficiency is associated with impaired repair, but the mitochondrion-to-nucleus intermediates remain unresolved.
Deficient fibroblasts accumulate ROS under oxidative-phosphorylation-dependent culture conditions.
Normoxic deficient fibroblasts accumulate nuclear HIF-1α through an unresolved signal.
Fewer assembled complexes reduce cytochrome c oxidase activity.
Complete COX4 loss in HEK293 cells disrupts mitochondrial translation; the exact assembly-to-translation signal is unresolved.
Deficient terminal electron transfer can limit oxidative ATP production.
Respiratory dysfunction is a plausible contributor to brain injury, although neural vulnerability was not directly tested in patient neurons.
Altered oxidative metabolism can favor lactate accumulation; normal lactate also occurs.
Cultures adapt to respiratory impairment by favoring glycolysis; the upstream signaling is not fully resolved.
The P152T siblings had encephalopathy as part of their central nervous system presentation.
Neurologic deterioration can cause loss of previously acquired developmental abilities; age and tempo vary.
Cognitive impairment accompanies severe neurodevelopmental involvement in some patients.
Cerebral involvement can manifest as epilepsy, with infantile seizure onset documented in the deletion/missense case.
The older P152T sibling developed infantile spasms with hypsarrhythmia at 12 months.
Central neurologic disease can contribute to hypotonia, although a peripheral or muscle contribution has not been excluded.
MRI demonstrates bilateral caudate and lenticular signal abnormalities in the later-onset neurologic presentation.
Progressive cerebral volume loss documents structural brain involvement in the deletion/missense case.
The later-onset motor disorder includes progressive lower-limb spasticity.
The later-onset case has a mixed spastic-dystonic movement disorder.
Involuntary orofacial movements occur in the later-onset neurologic presentation.
Orofacial motor dysfunction is associated with impaired pronunciation in the later-onset case.
Orofacial motor dysfunction is associated with swallowing difficulty in the later-onset case.
Impaired repair provides a candidate explanation for damage accumulating in proliferating deficient cells.
Cellular DNA damage provides a plausible link to the founding clinical breakage phenotype; the intermediate steps are not established.
Persistent DNA damage may contribute to reduced proliferation; alternative causes remain possible.
Reduced cellular proliferation may contribute to growth failure; this extrapolation has not been demonstrated in vivo.
HIF-1α-associated transcription is proposed to drive the compensatory isoform response.
Attenuated mitochondrial protein synthesis is a proposed contributor to complex I biogenesis failure in complete-knockout cells.
Swallowing dysfunction can compromise safe and adequate feeding.
Inadequate oral intake can contribute to poor weight gain.
